As of 252 PM EDT Monday...

KEY MESSAGE 1: A cold front will be dropping southward this
evening with rain chances increasing overnight as the parent low
ejects into the northern Atlantic off eastern Canada. The result
will be for the boundary to stall out over the region for
Tuesday through Tuesday night as another fast moving clipper
style system approaches from the west. This wave will increase 
southerly flow across the quasi-stationary boundary deepening 
moisture advection and increasing isentropic lift across the 
boundary. This will result in an extended period of wet 
conditions for the Adirondacks and north/central Vermont.
Initial rainfall will favor upslope areas of the Adirondacks 
and the northern Greens with westerly flow aloft. However, 
overnight into Tuesday, flow turns more southerly and deepens 
promoting strong moisture advection across the stalled boundary.
This flow direction will result in increased precipitation 
amounts with a lack of shadowing. As such, precipitation amounts
were increased area wide, with lowest totals around 0.5" 
towards southern Vermont to 1-2 inches tonight through Tuesday 
night from central Vermont northward. Highest amounts will be 
over the northern Greens and Adirondacks, but 1-1.75" is 
possible even for lower elevations in northern Vermont and 
northern New York. A few thunderstorms will be possible, 
especially Tuesday morning with a trough sweeping through and 
again Tuesday afternoon with the low approaching. This setup may
promote some cold air damming east of the Greens, with highs 
Tuesday below 50 degrees in northeastern Vermont. 

KEY MESSAGE 2: As the boundary drops southward this evening
winds in the northern Champlain Valley will briefly increase
with northerly winds of 15 to 25 mph and some gusts to around 30
mph across Lake Champlain. These winds will drop after midnight.
Next, a low level jet that will amplify the moisture across the
stationary boundary will move through Tuesday increasing
southerly flow mainly for the northern Champlain Valley since
moisture will dampen wind potential. Mixing over the lake may be
sufficient to intermittently bring some of these moderate gusts
to around 30 mph down to the lake surface. Finally, a stronger
push Wednesday will shunt the stationary boundary southward with
northerly breezes developing behind a reinforcing boundary.
Gusts 20 to 35 mph will be possible with stronger ridge level
winds expected. 

KEY MESSAGE 3: A northern stream Alberta clipper will phase with a 
southern stream closed low leading to an amplifying strong shortwave 
by early Friday. Widespread rain is expected Friday before 
temperatures sharply cool Friday night with the potential to see a 
switch to terrain snow showers Friday night into Saturday. Widespread 
rainfall amounts above half an inch are likely with 80-100% ensemble 
probabilities of 0.5 inches or more on Friday before any 
precipitation transitions to a rain snow mix in the terrain. Trends 
continue to denote likely probabilities of an inch or more with 60-
90% chances across the Adirondacks, and much of central and northern 
Vermont as well. Consensus favors our northern zones as the focus of 
the highest precipitation amounts with this system. 

A cold front will sweep through the area Friday night sharply 
lowering temperatures 10 to 15 degrees from Friday evening to 
Saturday morning. Temperatures will likely dip below freezing for 
most if not all locations across the area with only those near Lake 
Champlain and immediately near the St. Lawrence River staying above 
freezing. As temperatures fall, snow levels during the day Saturday 
will also lower to 500-1000ft agl, with a transition to snow above 
1500ft agl, and a rain, wet snow mix, in elevations between 1000-
1500ft agl. A few mixed in flurries cannot be ruled our even in the 
Champlain Valley, though temperatures will be marginal in the mid to 
upper 30s. Some snowliage appears likely with ensembles denoting 
nearly 100% chances for purely snowfall in the Adirondacks and 
Northeast Kingdom. Snowfall impacts will be minimal with road 
temperatures well above freezing, and with only marginal surface 
temperatures, snow will likely be of a wet character, with minor 
accumulation only on the highest elevations and mainly on vegetation 
only. Most locations will not see any accumulations at this point. 

Rain and snow showers will taper off Saturday evening as the system 
pulls away to the northeast. 850 mb temperatures Saturday night will 
be remarkably cold for this time of year in the -9 to -11C range 
Saturday night supporting temperatures in the 20s for most of the 
area, including the entire Champlain Valley. Pockets of teens will 
be possible in the coldest hollows of the Adirondacks and Northeast 
Kingdom as surface temperatures anomalies will be 10 degrees below 
normal. Temperatures will slowly moderate back towards seasonable 
normals to start next week.
